# 1 Chronicles 27: verse-by-verse research notes

**What I couldn't find:** My searches turned up nothing on this chapter from bibleodyssey.org, the netbible.org study notes, newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org. A search for Haydock's Catholic commentary found only other chapters. I also found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter. None of the sources set out denominational differences either. Where commentators disagree, it's between individual writers, mostly about the Hebrew text and the census. I've marked those disagreements below.

---

**Overview (vv. 1–34)**
- Constable says David organised his army, tribal leaders, administrators and counsellors to secure stability, so that what God had promised could happen "without unnecessary opposition or confusion." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/27-1.html
- Guzik's summary: David's greatness came from careful running of his kingdom as well as from his victories. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-27/

**v. 1**
- Ellicott: "their officers" were scribes who kept the muster rolls. "Divisions" uses the same Hebrew word as the Levite groups in the chapters before. Each month, the division on duty stood under arms as a kind of national guard. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/27-1.htm
- JFB: there were 24 captains of thousands and 240 captains of hundreds. In an emergency the whole force could be called up, about 288,000 to 300,000 men. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/27-1.htm
- Gill (listed as a Calvinist Baptist) says this was the nation's militia, not the whole people. It was set up early in David's reign, which explains Asahel's place in the list. Serving one month a year was no great burden. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/27-1.html
- Keil & Delitzsch don't think the division on duty was brought to the capital. They take it to mean the men were ready to obey orders while the rest of the army gathered. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-chronicles-27.html
- Wesley: the system trained nearly 300,000 men to use weapons while guarding against sudden uprisings or invasions. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-chronicles-27.html
- Guzik: Israel didn't rely on hired foreign soldiers; Israelites served the king themselves. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-27/
- **A different view:** G. Campbell Morgan suggests these officers may have been labourers working on the Temple, and that all of David's late arrangements served the Temple. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-27-commentary
- Applications: Coke says we should always be ready for spiritual warfare. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tcc/1-chronicles-27.html Matthew Henry says being watchful in war secures peace, and carelessness invites Satan's attacks. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/27-4.htm

**vv. 2–3**
- Kennicott, as cited by the Pulpit Commentary, thinks a phrase in 2 Samuel 23:8 is a copying error for the name "Jashobeam." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/27.htm
- Gill: the first month was Nisan. Jashobeam was the chief of David's mighty men and, as a descendant of Perez, had first rank. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/27-4.htm
- Ryrie notes that eight of the twelve generals were from Judah. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-27-commentary

**v. 4**
- Several commentators think "Eleazar son of" has dropped out before Dodai, comparing 1 Chronicles 11:12 and 2 Samuel 23:9. These include Barnes, JFB and the Pulpit Commentary. Barnes adds a Jewish tradition that Eleazar was David's cousin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/27-4.htm
- **Debated:** who Mikloth was. Benson and Poole offer three options: Dodai's successor, his deputy, or a notable officer in the division. The Geneva Bible says deputy. Cambridge notes the words are missing from the Septuagint and calls them corrupt. The Pulpit Commentary thinks the Hebrew text is probably faulty. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/27-4.htm

**v. 5**
- **Debated:** "Jehoiada the priest." Clarke, Benson and Coke take *cohen* here to mean "prince" or "chief officer," since Benaiah was never a priest. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/1-chronicles-27.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tcc/1-chronicles-27.html
- Keil, as cited by the Pulpit Commentary, thinks the word "chief" belongs with Benaiah, not with "priest." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/27.htm
- An ISBE note on Precept Austin observes that 1 Chronicles 12:27 names a Jehoiada as leader of the house of Aaron. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-27-commentary

**v. 6**
- Guzik recalls Benaiah's exploits from 2 Samuel 23:20–21: he killed two Moabite warriors, a lion in a pit on a snowy day, and an Egyptian. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-27/

**v. 7**
- Asahel was killed by Abner long before this list was written (2 Samuel 2:18–23). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-27/
- Keil: the words "his son after him" point to Asahel's death. Naming Asahel was an honour; his son's division kept the dead father's name. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-chronicles-27.html
- The Homiletical Commentary draws a lesson about the lasting value of a good name. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/27-1.html

**vv. 8–15**
- If Shamhuth is the Shammoth or Shammah of the other lists, he may have taken "Izrahite" from an ancestor (Treasury of Scripture Knowledge, TSK). For v. 10, Pelonite matches "Paltite" in 2 Samuel 23:26. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-27-commentary
- Bridgeway: all twelve commanders came from David's group of mighty men (1 Chronicles 11). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/27-1.html

**vv. 16–22**
- Keil: the tribal princes come right after the army because they ran the people's internal affairs. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-chronicles-27.html
- Wesley: these princes seem to have ranked above the army captains and were probably the king's chief counsellors. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-chronicles-27.html
- Guzik: they were civil administrators, not priests or soldiers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-27/
- **Debated:** why Gad and Asher are missing. Clarke, quoted by Guzik, thinks their entries were probably lost. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-27/ Wesley thinks Gad may have been joined with Reuben under one prince. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-chronicles-27.html The Pulpit Commentary compares this with the omission of Dan and Zebulun elsewhere. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-27.html

**v. 23**
- Keil: David numbered only men over twenty. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-chronicles-27.html
- Wesley: counting everyone would have been endless work and would have tempted God by questioning his promise. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-chronicles-27.html
- Pulpit: God had already given his people the proudest description of their numbers, that they would be countless. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-27.html
- **A different reading:** a note on Precept Austin suggests Joab may have begun counting children too. Counting fighting men might be sound policy, but counting children could only come from pride. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64115/

**v. 24**
- **Debated:** how to view David here. Guzik says David *wisely* stopped the census and trusted God's promise. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-27/ The Biblical Illustrator calls it "royal folly," since David insisted against Joab's advice. The Homiletical Commentary sees God holding back David's will. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/27-1.html
- Precept Austin: God allowed Satan to prompt David. A census wasn't wrong in itself, but this one showed David trusting in numbers rather than in God. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-27-commentary
- Bible Hub's study note: David's own records refuse to keep a figure linked to sin and judgment. https://biblehub.com/1_chronicles/27-24.htm

**v. 25**
- Pulpit: the same Hebrew word covers precious treasure in the first half of the verse and grain or produce in the second. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/27.htm
- Keil: "the king's treasuries" were the palace treasures in Jerusalem. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-chronicles-27.html
- JFB: grain was often stored in the fields under earth mounds. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/1-chronicles-27.html

**vv. 26–27**
- Wesley: one officer oversaw the workers and another the produce, in both fields (v. 26) and vineyards (v. 27). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-chronicles-27.html
- Keil: Shimei came from Ramah in Benjamin, and the wine stores were probably in Judah. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-chronicles-27.html
- Pulpit: "Shiphmite" may refer to Shepham (Numbers 34:10–11). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-27.html

**v. 28**
- Pulpit: the sycamore here is the fig-mulberry, a common tree that was useful to the poor. Baal-hanan is also the name of an Edomite king. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/27.htm

**v. 29**
- Pulpit: Sharon means "the level land," pasture stretching from Carmel to Joppa. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-27.html

**vv. 30–31**
- Pulpit: "Obil" means a camel-keeper, a job that suited an Ishmaelite. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/27.htm
- Clarke, quoted by Guzik: an Arab over the camels and a Hagrite (from a shepherd people) over the flocks shows nothing went by favour. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-27/
- Pulpit: these officials again number twelve. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/27.htm
- Wesley and Benson: there are no officials for show or sport, only for running the estate. David was a great soldier and scholar, "and yet a great husband of his estate." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-chronicles-27.html
- F. B. Meyer, quoted by Guzik: the officials managed what belonged to the king and must not treat it as their own. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-27/
- Meyer, on Precept Austin, links the list to 1 Corinthians 12 (many gifts, one Lord). https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-27-commentary

**v. 32**
- **Debated:** "uncle." Some take the word to mean "nephew" or simply "relative," identifying Jonathan with the son of David's brother Shimea (1 Chronicles 20:7). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/1-chronicles-27.html The Pulpit Commentary objects that the word means "uncle" every other time it is used that way. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/27.htm
- Wesley: a "scribe" here means either an expert in God's law or the king's secretary. Jehiel was the princes' tutor. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-chronicles-27.html
- Pulpit: if Jehiel was a son of Hachmoni, he may have been related to Jashobeam. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_chronicles/27.htm

**v. 33**
- Precept Austin: Ahithophel was a trusted counsellor who betrayed David for Absalom, then took his own life when Absalom followed Hushai's plan instead of his. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64115/
- JFB: the Septuagint calls Hushai the king's "first friend." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/1-chronicles-27.html

**v. 34**
- Wesley: after Ahithophel died, these men became David's chief counsellors. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-chronicles-27.html
- **Debated:** "Jehoiada son of Benaiah." The Homiletical Commentary thinks he was probably named after his grandfather. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/27-1.html Some commentators, following two manuscripts, read "Benaiah son of Jehoiada" instead, as the ISBE note on Precept Austin reports. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-27-commentary
- Guzik calls Joab one of the Old Testament's more complex characters: cunning, ruthless, and willing to disobey David when he thought it was for David's good. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-27/
